extracted.intended_audience: news editors, recommender-system designers, media scholars, and journalists interested in news selection and framing effects
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply criteria from Iyengar's episodic vs. thematic framing research to evaluate or design news-selection (e.g., homepage/recommender) systems; focuses on how frame form affects attribution, coverage probability, and engagement. Useful for editors, product teams, and researchers operationalizing frameability as a feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete, case-based, often visual reporting that illustrates issues through individual cases (e.g., a homeless person, a single victim, a specific crime, a single school shooting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High emotional engagement; 'passing parade of specific events.' Suits short visual formats (TV 90-second slots). Tends to produce narrative closure and personalization. Anti-pattern: treating systemic problems only through isolated anecdotes without context; may encourage individual-level causal attributions (e.g., poverty due to laziness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregated, contextual, statistical reporting that presents collective evidence about issues (e.g., unemployment rates, poverty distributions, structural school problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower visual appeal and more abstract; requires longer treatment to convey context and causes. Encourages societal or governmental attribution for problems (e.g., policy failure, economic conditions). Anti-pattern: presenting only statistics without humanizing detail where needed for comprehension or engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for stories that yield photographable or filmable individual victims/heroes versus stories that are mainly statistical or structural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories with a clear visual subject are more likely to be selected for coverage. Operational note: 'visualizability' can be used as a feature in homepage/recommender models. Anti-pattern: excluding important statistical stories because they lack immediate visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that generate strong emotional responses—typically single-case, human-interest pieces—are preferred because they attract viewers/readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional intensity correlates with ratings/clicks; editors prioritize pieces that provoke affect. For product teams, consider engagement uplift versus civic information value. Anti-pattern: optimizing solely for short-term engagement at the expense of public-information goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that present a clear beginning, middle, and end (single cases) are favored over stories about ongoing structural conditions that lack neat closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closure aids story-telling and audience comprehension in short formats. Consider whether forcing closure on structural issues misrepresents complexity. Anti-pattern: truncating systemic issues into oversimplified case narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-slot compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Suitability of a story for constrained broadcast or editorial slots (e.g., 90-second TV segments); episodic stories fit short slots better than thematic ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format constraints drive selection: short slots bias toward episodic content. For homepage/recommender design, surface length/format as a selection constraint and consider mechanisms to surface thematic pieces requiring longer attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ease of locating and interviewing individual sources (victims, witnesses, heroes) compared to assembling and interpreting aggregated data or expert commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories with readily available interviewees are more likely to be produced. Editorial workflows should account for resource costs of producing thematic pieces (data work, expert sourcing). Anti-pattern: ignoring important stories because sourcing is more effortful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization premium
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency (per Galtung & Ruge and related criteria) for personalization to increase newsworthiness—individual-centered stories receive preferential treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalization nearly automatically raises a story's appeal to news-selectors. Consider balancing personalization with civic-importance heuristics to avoid skewed coverage priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frameability (form-driven selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an event or issue can be framed episodically (case-based) vs. thematically (structural) determines its eligibility for coverage; form is itself a selection bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story resists episodic treatment it is systematically under-covered. Operationally, 'frameability' is a measurable feature that predicts coverage probability and engagement; editorial policies or algorithms should explicitly account for frame bias to correct under-coverage of structural issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution effect of frame type
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic framing leads viewers to attribute causes to individuals (individual attribution), whereas thematic framing leads to societal or governmental attributions (structural attribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a causal effect shown experimentally: choice of frame shifts public responsibility attributions without viewer awareness. Use this understanding when evaluating downstream civic effects of coverage (e.g., support for policy vs. personal-blame solutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invisibility of framing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame choice operates without viewer awareness; audience members typically do not recognize that framing is shaping their attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because effects are covert, designers and editors cannot rely on audience correction; responsibility lies with producers and platforms to mitigate unintended attributional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage bias against diffuse/structural problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural or diffuse social problems receive coverage primarily when they erupt into visible individual cases; otherwise they remain under-covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This results in attention cycles that privilege episodic manifestations; editorial strategies should proactively surface thematic/contextual reporting to counteract this bias. For recommender systems, include mechanisms to boost non-episodic important stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicts reform-resistance bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Because episodic framing localizes blame to individuals, news coverage shaped by episodic bias tends to favor personal-virtue solutions and disfavors policy reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating news impact or designing ranking/prioritization, measure whether framing patterns systematically lower public support for structural reforms; consider counterweights in curation to protect civic discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizability for homepage/recommender models
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing (episodic vs. thematic) is a measurable feature with predictive value for engagement metrics and attributional consequences; thus it can be used in homepage selection models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: label or predict frame-type as a feature, track its correlation with engagement and civic outcomes, and design constraints or diversification rules to avoid over-weighting episodic content. Consider trade-offs between engagement and public-information goals.
